common_name: Star of the East Crocosmia (Large-Flowered Apricot-Orange Montbretia)
scientific_name: Crocosmia x crocosmiiflora 'Star of the East'

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil after the danger of frost has passed.

directions: Star of the East stands out among crocosmias for its unusually large, wide-open flowers in soft apricot-orange with a golden throat, produced on gracefully arching stems well above the sword-shaped foliage. It multiplies steadily from cormlets each season, so clumps should be lifted and divided every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous. Grow it in a sunny border with reliably moist, fertile soil; in colder zones mulch heavily or lift corms for winter storage. Its oversized blooms and softer color make it a favorite for cutting and for pairing with hotter-hued red crocosmia cultivars.

common_name: Jackanapes Crocosmia (Bicolor Red and Yellow Montbretia)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in full sun once soil has warmed after the last frost.

directions: Jackanapes is one of the most distinctive crocosmia cultivars grown, bred by Alan Bloom, with striking bicolor blooms of rich red-orange outer segments surrounding a bright golden-yellow center. The zigzag flower spikes are shorter and stiffer than many montbretia hybrids, making the clumps sturdy and less prone to flopping. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain the strongest color contrast. Its compact size and bold two-tone flowers make it a striking front-of-border accent or container specimen.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost date.

directions: Severn Sunrise offers a softer palette than most crocosmias, with pale apricot-pink flowers that open from coral-orange buds and fade toward cream at the base of each petal. Bred by plantsman Eric Smith, it holds its unusual coloring best with some afternoon shade in hot climates, though full sun elsewhere yields the sturdiest stems. Keep soil consistently moist through the growing season and divide crowded clumps in spring every three to four years. The gentle pastel tones make it easy to combine with blues and purples in a mixed perennial border, unlike the typical hot reds and oranges of the genus.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil once frost danger has passed.

directions: Norwich Canary is a long-grown heirloom crocosmia valued for its clear, unshaded golden-yellow flowers, a cleaner color than the bronze-tinted yellows of many other cultivars. It forms upright clumps of pleated, sword-like foliage and produces branching flower spikes over a long summer bloom period. Give it full sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil, and divide every few years as cormlets multiply and crowd the clump. Its pure yellow color makes it a useful bridge between hot red and orange crocosmias and cooler-toned border companions.

common_name: Professor Barnard Crimson Flag Lily (Deep Carmine-Red Hesperantha)

planting.note: Divide and plant rhizomes in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Professor Barnard is a richly colored crimson flag lily cultivar, bearing deep carmine-red, star-shaped flowers on wiry stems well into autumn, later in the season than many perennials are still blooming. It forms grassy, evergreen-in-mild-climates clumps that spread steadily where soil stays reliably moist, making it well suited to pond margins, stream banks, or rain garden edges. Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering. Its intense red coloring is deeper and more saturated than the pinks common in the species, making it a striking late-season accent among ornamental grasses or ferns.

common_name: Viscountess Byng Crimson Flag Lily (Late-Blooming Pale Pink Hesperantha)

planting.note: Divide and plant rhizomes in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Viscountess Byng is one of the latest-flowering crimson flag lily cultivars, holding off until well into autumn to open its pale, soft-pink, star-shaped blooms, often continuing until the first hard frost cuts them down. Its late timing makes it valuable for extending color in the perennial border after most other bloomers have finished. Grow it in consistently moist soil near pond edges or in rain gardens, and divide clumps every three years in spring to keep flowering strong. The delicate pink flowers pair well with ornamental grasses and asters that share its autumn bloom window.
